passages.where: A saying so true that Proverbs repeats it word for word in 26:22. Gossip is pictured as food: a delicacy that is pleasant to take in and goes down deep. The proverb is honest about why gossip is hard to resist. It tastes good.

In a cluster of sayings about people who scheme against others, the gossip appears beside the troublemaker who stirs up strife. What the gossip divides is not strangers but close friends. Talk about someone behind their back eats away at the trust that holds people together.

This saying belongs to a portrait of the meddler and the quarreler. A fire dies when no one adds wood; a quarrel dies when no one carries the story further. Every listener has a choice about whether to be the next piece of wood.

In the chapter that calls Israel to be holy as God is holy, the ban on going about spreading slander sits between fair judgment in court and the command to love your neighbor as yourself. Speech about others is a matter of holiness. The next verse adds the alternative: if your neighbor has wronged you, speak to him directly.

The psalm asks who may live in God's presence, and the answer is a portrait of an honest person. Near the top of the list are truth spoken from the heart, no slander on the tongue, and no scorn cast on a friend. The way we speak of people when they are absent is part of how we stand before God.

James draws on images every reader knew: a bit in a horse's mouth, a ship's rudder, a spark in the dry summer hills. The tongue is small and sets great things on fire. James includes himself among those who stumble in speech, and says no one can fully tame it.

James sets two tests of real religion side by side. One is care for orphans and widows in their distress; the other is a bridled tongue. A person who speaks carelessly and thinks himself religious is deceiving himself.

The Pharisees have just said Jesus drives out demons by the prince of demons. He answers that a tree is known by its fruit, and that the mouth speaks out of what fills the heart. Words are not accidents; they show what is inside.

Paul pictures the Christian life as taking off old clothes and putting on new ones. The first new garment is truthfulness, and the reason is that we are members of one another. Lying to or about a fellow believer is like one part of a body deceiving another.
Paul is speaking of how believers talk with people outside the church. Speech is to be gracious and seasoned with salt: kind, but with flavor and substance, fitted to the person in front of you.
In a chapter full of sayings about lying and truthful lips, this one sets two kinds of words side by side. Rash words pierce like a sword. The tongue of the wise heals. The same organ can do either.

misread.taken: Warnings against gossip and praise for keeping a confidence have been used to silence people who report abuse, wrongdoing or danger, as if telling a pastor, a counselor or the police were the sin of gossip.
misread.says: The proverb contrasts a person who goes about revealing secrets with one who can be trusted. Gossip is talk that harms a person for the pleasure or advantage of the one talking. Telling the truth to someone who can protect a person or stop a wrong is a different act altogether. Leviticus 19, which forbids spreading slander, also forbids endangering a neighbor's life, and commands speaking to a wrongdoer directly. Reporting harm to those who can act is never gossip.

misread.taken: This verse is used as a ban on any critical, uncomfortable or negative speech, so that naming a problem or disagreeing with someone is treated as unwholesome talk.
misread.says: Paul asks for speech that builds up the one in need and gives grace to those who hear. Building up can include correction and hard truth; four verses earlier he has told the church to speak truthfully, and in the same letter to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). The test is not whether words feel pleasant but whether they serve the real good of the person, and whether they are said to the one who needs to hear them rather than about them.

whole: Gossip rarely feels like sin while it is happening. It feels like concern, or like keeping someone informed, or like a little relief after a hard week. It usually begins with a sentence that sounds kind: I'm only telling you because I'm worried. Most people have been hurt by it, and most have done it, and many have felt the strange pull of a story about someone else, the way Proverbs says, like a delicacy that goes down easily.

Scripture treats speech as one of the clearest windows into a person. Jesus says the mouth speaks from what fills the heart, and James says a person who cannot bridle the tongue is deceived about their own religion. The Bible's concern is not only with lies. Leviticus forbids going about spreading slander, Psalm 15 counts it against anyone who would live in God's presence, and Proverbs notices what gossip does over time: it separates close friends and keeps quarrels burning. Under all of it is something Paul names plainly. We are members of one another, and words spoken about someone in their absence wound the body they belong to.

The cause is often less malice than appetite. Gossip lets us feel close to one person by stepping back from another, feel better about ourselves by comparison, or feel important for knowing. It can be a way of complaining without having the hard conversation. That is why the Bible's alternative is not silence but a different kind of speech. Leviticus pairs the ban on slander with the command to rebuke a neighbor directly. Jesus teaches that if someone sins against you, you go to them first. And no warning against gossip may ever be used to stop someone from telling a pastor, a counselor or the police that a person is being harmed.

So the wisdom here starts with small habits. Notice the first sentence of gossip, in your own mouth and in others', and let it stop with you; a fire goes out without wood. Ask before you speak of someone absent whether you would say it the same way with them in the room. Speak to people rather than about them. Where you have done damage, go back and repair it. And remember that the tongue that can set a forest on fire can also heal. Gracious speech, seasoned with salt, is not weaker speech. It is speech that has decided whose good it serves.

differ.share: Christians agree that the tongue must be governed, that lies and slander are sin, that truth is to be spoken in love, and that correcting a brother or sister is sometimes a duty.

views.name: Gentleness as the rule
views.body: Many Christians stress that the New Testament asks believers to answer with gentleness and respect, to correct opponents with patience, and to give the benefit of the doubt. They see sharp words as the rare exception, held back for clear and serious wrong, and wary of anyone who enjoys them.

views.name: Plain rebuke has its place
views.body: Other Christians stress that the prophets, Jesus in his woes to the Pharisees, and Paul opposing Peter to his face all spoke bluntly when truth or the vulnerable were at stake. They see a preference for pleasant speech as a way churches avoid hard truth, and hold that love sometimes sounds severe.

differ.after: This is less a division between churches than a difference of conviction and temperament inside them. Both agree that the test of hard words is whether they are spoken to the person, for their good, and with no pleasure in their pain.

sit: Whom have you spoken about this month in a way you would not have spoken with them present, and what would it take to go to them instead?

prayer.lead: A song of ascents from someone surrounded by lying tongues. Pray it if you are the one being talked about, and let it search you if you have been the one talking.
